opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the main reason is that mathematics today is extremely fragmented. There are so many subfields, and each one has its own language, its own techniques, its own folklore. A researcher in optimization and a researcher in, say, algebraic geometry might be working on problems that are secretly related, but neither of them would ever know, because it takes years to become fluent enough in another area to recognize that connection. Human attention is the bottleneck.

AI changes that, because these models have, in some sense, read everything. They aren't experts at the level of the very best person in each field, at least not yet, but they have broad familiarity across all of it. So when I'm stuck on a problem, I can ask a model, and it might say, "This looks like a technique from such-and-such area," and point me toward a lemma I never would have encountered on my own. I've had that experience personally. Sometimes the suggestion is wrong, but often it's a real lead, and a few hours of checking can save months of reinventing something that already exists.

I think there's a second effect too. Right now a lot of results are effectively lost. They're buried in a paper from the 1980s, or written in notation nobody uses anymore, and the community simply forgets them. AI can resurface that work and translate it into a form that's usable today. That makes the whole body of mathematical knowledge feel more connected and alive, rather than a collection of isolated islands.

And finally, as tools like formal verification and AI-assisted proving mature, it becomes easier to collaborate across boundaries, because you can trust a result from a field you don't fully understand. You don't have to personally verify every step. That lowers the barrier to building on other people's work. So I see AI less as replacing mathematicians and more as connective tissue, helping individual researchers see a much larger portion of the mathematical landscape than any one person could on their own.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can resurface results buried in older papers and translate them into a form usable today.

r002.rationale: It describes asking a model for help and being pointed to techniques and lemmas from areas the researcher would not otherwise have encountered.

r003.rationale: The response mentions checking suggestions, but does not clearly distinguish discovering a result with AI from the further study needed to apply it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that mathematics has become so specialized that most of us live in very narrow rooms. I work in optimization and machine learning theory, and if you handed me a paper in, say, algebraic geometry, I could spend a month just learning the vocabulary before I understood whether it was relevant to anything I care about. That's not a failure of individual mathematicians. It's just that the literature is enormous and a human lifetime is short.

What struck me when I started seriously using these models on research problems is that they don't have that constraint. They've read everything. So when I'm stuck on something, the model will sometimes say, in effect, "this looks like a known structure in a field you've never touched," and point me at a result or a technique I had no way of knowing existed. Sometimes it's wrong, and I have to check carefully. But sometimes it's right, and that's a connection that simply would not have been made otherwise, because the two people who could have made it were never in the same room.

I think that's the big shift. Historically, the great unifying moments in mathematics came from rare individuals who happened to know two fields deeply. AI lowers the cost of that enormously. A graduate student in one area can now reach into another area and actually get traction, with the model acting as a translator and a guide to the literature.

And I'd add one more thing. A lot of the value of mathematics is in the small lemmas and techniques that never get famous. They sit in some paper from 1987 and nobody cites them. These systems surface that material. So I don't think the future is AI replacing mathematicians. I think it's mathematicians finally being able to use the whole body of mathematics, instead of the small corner each of us managed to learn.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems surface obscure small lemmas and techniques from old, uncited papers when researchers are stuck and need a connection.

r002.rationale: It describes models pointing researchers to results in fields they have never touched and helping a graduate student reach into another area.

r003.rationale: The response calls the model a translator and guide, but does not clearly state that researchers still need to study a discovered result in order to apply it.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the exciting things about mathematics is that an idea developed in one area can turn out to be exactly what you need in another. But those connections are difficult to find, because each of us can understand only a small part of the mathematical literature. Different fields also develop different languages, so two people can be studying closely related structures without realizing it.

AI could help us bridge those gaps. You might be working on a problem and have an AI point out, “There’s a technique in this other field that could be relevant,” and then help you understand it in your own language. You still have to check whether the connection is meaningful and whether the argument is correct. But it opens up possibilities you might never have considered.

So I’m excited about more than solving existing problems faster. I’m excited about discovering new questions and new relationships between subjects. That could make mathematics richer by helping us see how ideas fit together.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could surface a technique from another field when it becomes relevant to a problem, addressing results that researchers might otherwise overlook.

r002.rationale: It describes AI pointing researchers toward relevant techniques in other fields they may not know, and helping them understand those techniques.

r003.rationale: The response says researchers must check whether a connection is meaningful and an argument is correct, but does not clearly state that they still need to study a discovered result to apply it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most exciting things about mathematics is that ideas developed in one area can turn out to be exactly what you need in another. But those connections are hard to find, because each field has its own language, its own intuitions, and an enormous literature. No individual can absorb all of that.

AI could help us cross those boundaries. You might describe a problem, and it could suggest, “There’s a construction in another field that looks very much like this.” That doesn’t solve the problem automatically, but it gives you a new perspective—a connection you might otherwise never have encountered.

And if we can make it easier for people to learn the background needed to follow those connections, more people can participate. So I don’t just imagine mathematics becoming faster. I imagine more ideas coming into contact, more people being able to work together, and new questions emerging from those interactions. Of course, we still have to check the arguments. A plausible connection is a starting point, not a proof.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can surface a construction from another field that fits a problem and may otherwise go unnoticed, making it useful when needed.

r002.rationale: It describes AI helping people cross mathematical boundaries and find a relevant construction in another field, despite no individual being able to absorb all fields’ literature.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes AI suggesting a connection from solving the problem: people still need background to follow the connection and must check the arguments.
